blocks.content: Beyond the basic layer reuse covered earlier, Docker's build cache has real tooling around it, flags to bypass it, mechanisms to persist package manager caches across builds, and ways to share cache across entirely separate CI machines.
1. Cache Reuse Is On by Default
blocks.text: 1. Cache Reuse Is On by Default

blocks.content: Every docker build automatically tries to reuse cached layers wherever the instruction and its input have not changed, no flag is needed to opt into this, it is the default, cache-aware behavior of every build.

blocks.alt: Cache reuse happens automatically, no flag needed

blocks.content: Sometimes you genuinely need to bypass the cache entirely, a suspicion that a cached layer is stale in a way Docker cannot detect (an ADD from a URL whose content changed, for instance). --no-cache forces every instruction to actually re-execute.

blocks.alt: Every instruction re-executes, nothing is reused

blocks.content: 3. Persisting Package Manager Caches with Cache Mounts
blocks.text: 3. Persisting Package Manager Caches with Cache Mounts

blocks.content: A BuildKit feature, RUN --mount=type=cache, lets a specific directory (like npm's or pip's download cache) persist across builds even when the surrounding layer itself gets invalidated, meaningfully speeding up dependency installs on every build after the first, cache-busted layer or not.

blocks.alt: A package manager cache survives even a busted layer

blocks.content: A fresh CI runner typically starts with zero local Docker cache, every build is effectively a --no-cache build unless you do something about it. --cache-from (and BuildKit's --cache-to for exporting) let a pipeline pull previously built layers from a registry, giving even a brand new runner a warm cache to build from.

blocks.alt: A registry-backed cache gives ephemeral runners a warm start
Exporting cache to a registry for the next build to import

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: The build cache is automatic by default, --no-cache is the deliberate escape hatch when you need a genuinely clean rebuild.
Cache mounts persist package manager caches across builds, and --cache-from/--cache-to let CI pipelines share a warm cache through a registry.
